title: Organising maternity services and national policy
blurb: Map the settings, lead professionals and system structures of maternity care, and spot the staffing red flags that threaten safety.
question: At 3 am the labour ward coordinator realises one midwife is caring for two women in established labour. What does national guidance call this, and what should the coordinator do?

teach.h: Who leads, where, and who decides
teach.body: Formally, maternity care is organised by setting (home, freestanding midwifery unit, alongside midwifery unit, obstetric unit), by lead professional (midwife-led or obstetric-led) and by a commissioning system that plans services for a population. In plain English: where she gives birth, who is in charge of her care, and who pays for and shapes the service are three separate questions, and midwives need to understand all three (SPM 2.1-2.3).

teach.caption: NG235 1.2.1: commissioners should make all four settings available to all women, locally or in a neighbouring area.

teach.h: Midwife-led, obstetric-led and transfer of care
teach.body: A midwife is the lead professional for women at low risk of complications, whatever the setting. Transfer of care means moving between midwifery-led and obstetric-led care. It may not involve any physical move: a woman having midwife-led care in an obstetric unit can become obstetric-led in the same room (NG235 1.5). Epidurals are given only in obstetric units.

Threshold
teach.caption: The midwife in charge decides whether staffing is the cause and what action to take.

teach.body: Bea finds one midwife caring for two women in established labour. NG235 1.4.5 asks services to provide a model of care that supports one-to-one care in labour for all women, 1.4.6 says not to leave a woman in established labour on her own except briefly, and NG4 lists losing one-to-one care as a red flag. Bea declares the red flag, follows the escalation policy (calling the on-call manager, redeploying staff, pausing elective work such as inductions), records the event and reports it so the staffing pattern can be reviewed. Safe staffing and skill mix underpin safety (SPM 5.5).

teach.text: 'Transfer of care' is about who LEADS care, not about an ambulance. And a woman in an alongside midwifery unit who wants an epidural needs transfer to the obstetric unit: no midwifery unit offers epidurals.

items: Settings: home, FMU, AMU, obstetric unit; all four should be available to all women.
Lead professional: midwife-led for low risk; transfer of care changes the lead, not necessarily the room.
England: ICBs commission, LMNS is the maternity arm of the ICS, MNVPs bring in women's voices.
Three-year plan themes: listening to women, workforce, safety culture, standards and structures.
NG4 red flags include losing one-to-one care in established labour: escalate.

summary: You can now describe the four birth settings, the difference between midwife-led and obstetric-led care, and how maternity services are commissioned and shaped in England. You can also recognise staffing red flags and respond to them.

A.q: Which birth setting is a midwife-led unit on the same site as an obstetric unit?
options: Alongside midwifery unit
Freestanding midwifery unit
Obstetric unit
Community birth centre
A.why: An alongside midwifery unit (AMU) is midwife-led and located on the same site as an obstetric unit, so obstetric care is close by.

whyNot.1: A freestanding unit is on a separate site from the obstetric unit.
whyNot.2: An obstetric unit is led by the obstetric team, not a midwife-led unit.
whyNot.3: This is not one of the four NICE settings and does not define co-location.

A.q: Which is one of the four themes of NHS England's three-year delivery plan for maternity and neonatal services (2023)?
options: Meeting a national target for caesarean rates
Moving all births into obstetric units by 2026
Expanding private provision of maternity care
Growing, retaining and supporting the workforce
A.why: Theme 2 is growing, retaining and supporting our workforce. The others are listening to women, a culture of safety, and standards and structures.

whyNot.0: The plan does not set a national caesarean rate target.
whyNot.1: The plan supports choice of all birth settings, not centralisation.
whyNot.2: Private provision is not a theme of the plan.

A.q: In England, which bodies commission most maternity services?
options: Integrated care boards
Local authorities
The Care Quality Commission
The Nursing and Midwifery Council
A.why: The three-year plan states that integrated care boards (ICBs) commission most maternity services, as partners in integrated care systems.

whyNot.1: Local authorities are not the commissioners of most maternity care; ICBs are.
whyNot.2: The CQC regulates and inspects services; it does not commission them.
whyNot.3: The NMC regulates midwives; it does not commission services.

B.q: Maria is having midwife-led care in a room on the obstetric unit. Meconium-stained liquor is noted and the obstetric registrar takes over her care. Which statement is correct?
options: Transfer of care has not occurred, as she stayed in the same room
Transfer of care has occurred, as her lead professional has changed
Transfer of care needs an ambulance to count as a transfer
Transfer of care applies to home births and freestanding units
B.why: NG235 defines transfer of care as moving between midwifery-led and obstetric-led care, which may or may not involve moving location.

whyNot.0: Location does not define transfer of care; the lead professional does.
whyNot.2: Transport is not required for a transfer of care.
whyNot.3: Transfer of care can happen in any setting, including the obstetric unit.

B.q: Which situation is a midwifery staffing red flag in NICE NG4?
options: A woman waits 20 minutes to be triaged
Perineal suturing is delayed by 45 minutes
Induction is delayed by 1 hour after admission
One-to-one care in established labour cannot be given
B.why: Any occasion when one midwife cannot provide continuous one-to-one care in established labour is an NG4 red flag.

whyNot.0: The triage red flag is a delay of 30 minutes or more.
whyNot.1: The suturing red flag is a delay of 60 minutes or more.
whyNot.2: The induction red flag is a delay of 2 hours or more.

B.q: What is the main purpose of a maternity and neonatal voices partnership (MNVP)?
options: To investigate serious maternity incidents
To inspect and rate local maternity units
To bring women's voices into service decisions
To hear fitness to practise cases about midwives
B.why: MNVPs, commissioned by ICBs, listen to and reflect the views of local communities and put service user voices at the heart of service improvement.

whyNot.0: Investigation is the role of bodies such as MNSI and trust processes under PSIRF.
whyNot.1: Inspection and rating is the CQC's role.
whyNot.3: Fitness to practise is the NMC's role.

C.q: At 3 am, coordinator Bea finds one midwife caring for two women in established labour. No other midwife is free. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Ask a student midwife to stay alone with one of the women
Wait to see whether either labour slows before acting
Declare a red flag and escalate under the staffing policy
Record the shortfall in the shift report at handover
C.why: Loss of one-to-one care in established labour is an NG4 red flag; the midwife in charge decides on action and escalates (for example, on-call manager, redeploying staff, pausing elective work).

whyNot.0: A student cannot replace a registered midwife's one-to-one care.
whyNot.1: Waiting leaves both women without safe care now.
whyNot.3: Recording alone does not fix the immediate risk; escalation is needed first.

C.q: Leah, at low risk, is labouring in an alongside midwifery unit and asks for an epidural. What should the midwife do?
options: Ask the anaesthetist to site it in the midwifery unit
Explain epidurals are not offered to women at low risk
Offer pethidine because the unit cannot give epidurals
Arrange transfer to the obstetric unit for the epidural
C.why: Epidurals are available only in obstetric units (NG235 1.6.26); a request for regional analgesia is a reason for transfer (NG235 1.2.2).

whyNot.0: Epidurals are not sited in midwifery units.
whyNot.1: Low-risk women can choose an epidural; it requires transfer.
whyNot.2: Pethidine is an option, but replacing her stated choice without offering transfer ignores it.

C.q: Better Births proposed that providers and commissioners work together in local maternity systems. What population size did it suggest these should cover?
options: 500,000 to 1.5 million
2 million to 3 million
5 million to 15 million
C.why: Better Births: local maternity systems covering populations of 500,000 to 1.5 million, with common standards and protocols.

whyNot.0: This is far smaller than the proposed systems.
whyNot.2: This exceeds the upper figure of 1.5 million.
whyNot.3: This is closer to a regional or network scale.

reteach.title: Three questions for every woman
reteach.question: Where is she giving birth, who leads her care, and who shapes the service around her?

blocks.body: Place: home, freestanding unit, alongside unit or obstetric unit. Lead: a midwife for low-risk care; an obstetric team when complications arise, which is a transfer of care even without a move. System: ICBs commission, the LMNS coordinates maternity and neonatal care, and MNVPs make sure women's voices are heard.

blocks.text: The CQC inspects, the NMC regulates midwives, and ICBs commission. Do not swap them.

explain.body: Four settings: home, FMU, AMU, OU. Midwife-led care is for women at low risk in any setting; obstetric-led care is for complications. Epidurals are given only in obstetric units.

test.q: Which statement about freestanding midwifery units is correct?
options: They are on the same site as an obstetric unit
They provide epidurals with anaesthetic cover
They are on a separate site from an obstetric unit
They are led by a consultant obstetrician
test.why: A freestanding midwifery unit is midwife-led and on a separate site, so transfer is needed for obstetric care.

whyNot.0: That describes an alongside midwifery unit.
whyNot.1: Epidurals are given only in obstetric units.

explain.body: ICBs commission most maternity services and fund MNVPs. The ICS is the wider partnership; the LMNS is its maternity and neonatal arm. MNVPs bring women's and families' views into decisions.

test.q: What is a local maternity and neonatal system (LMNS)?
options: The maternity and neonatal arm of the ICS
A national inspection body for maternity
A charity that supports bereaved parents
The regulator for midwifery education
test.why: The three-year plan describes the LMNS as the maternity and neonatal arm of the integrated care system.

whyNot.1: Inspection is done by the CQC, not the LMNS.

explain.body: Published 30 March 2023, four themes: listening to and working with women and families with compassion; growing, retaining and supporting the workforce; developing a culture of safety, learning and support; standards and structures for safer, more personalised and equitable care. All women are offered personalised care and support plans.

test.q: Under theme 1 of the three-year plan, what should all women be offered?
options: A home birth suitability assessment
A booking appointment with a consultant
A private single room after the birth
A personalised care and support plan
test.why: Theme 1 states that all women are offered personalised care and support plans, including a risk assessment updated at every contact.

whyNot.0: The plan supports choice but does not mandate a home birth assessment.
whyNot.1: Consultant review depends on need, not a universal offer.
whyNot.2: Single rooms are not a national commitment in the plan.

explain.body: Services should support one-to-one care in labour for all women and benchmark staffing using workforce models or ratios (NG235 1.4.5). NG4 red flags signal unsafe staffing; the midwife in charge decides on action. Staffing, skill mix and teamwork affect safety (SPM 5.5).

test.q: A woman in triage waits 35 minutes to be seen because all midwives are busy. How should this be classified?
options: A midwifery staffing red flag
Within the acceptable triage time
A reason to close the unit at once
An issue for the obstetric team
test.why: NG4 lists a delay of 30 minutes or more in triage as a red flag, which the midwife in charge must respond to.

whyNot.1: 35 minutes exceeds the 30-minute red flag threshold.
whyNot.2: Unit closure is a separate escalation decision, not automatic.
whyNot.3: Staffing red flags are managed by the midwife in charge.
